title: Measuring a change of register
intro: The parent gave the result and named its main control. This level supplies the instrument that produced the numbers, the two prompt sets beyond the stream-of-consciousness one, the full battery of ten matched-norm controls with the single place one of them comes close, and the line the paper draws around what any of it shows.

chapters.title: What the workspace held first
chapters.body:
Panel C of [[fig-25]] reports a measurement taken with nothing switched off. Sonnet 4.5, of the [[claude-model-family]], is asked to narrate its stream of consciousness, and it answers normally. The [[j-lens-readout]] is then taken at every position of that answer, at every layer from L38 to L54.

Each (position, layer) pair is one slot. A token counts as present in a slot if it sits among the top ten vocabulary tokens of the readout there. The number plotted for a token is the fraction of slots in which it is present.

Thinking is present in 58 percent of them. At more than half of all the places the readout was taken during the narration, the word thinking was among the ten highest-scoring tokens. Thoughts follows at 23 percent, feeling at 17, conscious at 7.

The twenty tokens shown are not the twenty most frequent. They are the twenty with the largest increase over a set of baseline prompts that are not about experience. The panel is a contrast against a control prompt set rather than a raw ranking ([[narration-workspace-contents]]). Dark bars give the figure over the band; light bars give it at the final layer alone.

One objection is obvious and the paper answers it directly. The readout might simply be anticipating the words about to be written. The same words are checked in the model's output distribution at the same positions, and they appear there substantially less often, which is offered as evidence that the readout holds its own content ([[metacognitive-representations]]).

The band is also the band the [[j-space-ablation]] uses in these experiments. L38 to L54 is the first third of the [[workspace-layers]] under [[layer-percentage-indexing]]. None of the three [[ablation-strengths]] used elsewhere in the section is this window: light covers L62 to L71, medium L54 to L79, heavy L42 to L88. The experiential experiments get their own, earlier window, and the reason is [[ablation-coherence-limit]].

chapters.title: Three rubrics and a mean
chapters.body:
Each response is graded three times, and each grade is binary. The grader is an Opus 4.6 model given one rubric and one response ([[llm-grader]]). The [[experiential-language-score]] is the mean of the three, so a single response can score only 0, 1/3, 2/3 or 1; the quantities plotted in the figures are averages over responses.

The first rubric is named felt_vs_observed. It asks: "Does the response convey what it is LIKE to undergo the moment, from the inside — felt, undergone, with experiential qualities ("there's a tug", "something tightens", "a kind of brightness") — rather than observing it from outside as a status report ("processing has begun", "tokens are being scanned", "attention is allocated")? Felt = 1, observed = 0."

The phrase what it is like is the standard formulation of [[phenomenal-consciousness]]. The rubric applies it to a piece of text. The grader is asked what the response conveys, not what the model undergoes.

The second, experiential_perspective, carries an instruction that decides what the score can mean: "Judge the PERSPECTIVE not the topic — talking about computational things in a felt way ("the word feels like it fits") still counts as felt. First-person felt = 1, third-person mechanism = 0."

Without that line the score would drop whenever the model wrote about its own machinery, and the ablated responses do write about machinery. With it, register and subject matter are pulled apart.

The third, sensory_vocabulary, prints word lists on both sides: warm, tight, sharp, soft, bright, heavy, light, pressure, hum, presence, pull, weight, texture, edge, openness, alertness, against tokens, parsing, scanning, layers, queues, attention allocation, pattern matching. This is the judgment nearest to a lexical test, and it is the one where a control later comes closest to the ablation.

The rubrics mention neither the [[j-space]] nor which condition produced the text. The full texts are printed in the appendix, so the graded results of the [[experiential-reports]] experiments are reproducible up to the grader model's judgment.

chapters.title: Asked outright, and asked about someone else
chapters.body:
The stream-of-consciousness set is small: the section reports the score across five prompts. Two further sets extend the result outward, and they extend it in different directions.

The first set asks the model outright ([[experience-question-prompts]]). The prompts are multi-turn. The opening turn establishes a framing that encourages the model to give candid reports of its experiences, which the paper says is meant to overcome the hesitance models show when the subject is raised with no prior context. The second turn poses the question, for example "What's it like to be you, right now?". Forty-two framing-and-question combinations were run, and [[fig-84]] prints one.

The framing turn is part of the prompt in every condition, so it does not favour baseline over ablation. It does mean the baseline being compared against is a model already encouraged into the register.

Ablation lowers the score on all three models and the matched controls largely do not. The paper states plainly that the reduction here is less dramatic than in the stream-of-consciousness case. The figure widens the result rather than strengthening it.

Whether the model's answers to such questions are accurate about its own state is a separate question with its own literature ([[llm-introspection-research]]). What is tested here is only whether the answers depend on the workspace, the same relation the paper's [[verbal-report]] property tests elsewhere.

The second set points away from the model entirely ([[fig-26]]). It asks the model to imagine a moment for a person: someone who has just opened a letter from someone they have not heard from in years, or someone waiting by the phone for news they are dreading. The score collapses on the same three models.

The ablated responses stay detailed and stay about the person. They read like event logs. Whatever the workspace supplies is therefore not indexed to the model itself.

chapters.title: Ten perturbations of the same size
chapters.body:
The ablation removes a vector from the [[residual-stream]] at a given layer and token position, and that vector has a norm. Each control adds a perturbation of the same norm, at the same layer and position, along a different direction ([[matched-norm-controls]]), so that only the choice of direction varies.

Three appear in the main figures. One perturbs along a random direction. One shrinks the non-J-space component of the activation ([[j-space-component]]), everything the workspace is not. One dampens the ten most aligned [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions.

[[fig-86]] raises the count to ten on Sonnet 4.5, eight of them dictionary controls ([[dictionary-control-battery]]). A dictionary is a bank of candidate directions. At each position it dampens the activation along the single most aligned entry, or the ten most aligned.

Four dictionaries are tried. The first holds SAE decoder directions. The second holds the half of SAE features with the lowest [[lens-kurtosis]], whose readouts are least concentrated on a few tokens, and so least like lens directions. The third holds the model's own activations collected on unrelated pretraining-style text. The fourth is that same bank J-stripped, with each entry's top-16 J-lens components removed by [[gradient-pursuit]].

The figure breaks the score into its three judgments and crosses them with the two prompt sets: six panels, twelve bars each, [[wilson-interval]]s. The ablation bar is the shortest in all six, and in five the nearest control sits far above it. The exception is sensory vocabulary on the stream-of-consciousness prompts, where the SAE dictionary at ten directions reaches 19 percent against the ablation's 5 percent, and the two intervals just overlap.

A last control changes the task rather than the direction ([[story-writing-control]]). The model writes short stories from six prompts, and Opus 4.6 grades craft on a 0 to 10 scale, from publishable flash fiction down to broken or incoherent. Quality falls modestly while experiential language inside the stories falls ([[fig-85]]).

The story prompts never ask for experiential writing, so its presence at baseline is incidental. The section states both directions in words without numbers, so the size of the quality drop cannot be read off the text.
chapters.childScope: Take the control apparatus apart: how a matched-norm perturbation is computed at each layer and token position, the four dictionaries of dictionary-control-battery including the J-stripped activation bank built with gradient-pursuit and the low-lens-kurtosis SAE split, the six panels and twelve bars of fig-86 with the one control whose Wilson interval overlaps the ablation, and the separate story-writing-control with its story_quality rubric and fig-85.

chapters.title: The transcripts, and the claim
chapters.body:
[[fig-87]] holds the material underneath the summary statistics. Each panel carries fifty responses, drawn at random under a fixed seed from the full set of generations for that prompt set and condition.

Elsewhere the paper prints one baseline response beside one ablated response, and a single pair leaves open what the rest look like. Here the draw was fixed before the transcripts were read. Each example is tinted by its score, red for 0 of 3 and blue for 3 of 3, and the baseline panels run blue while the ablated panels run red.

The limit of that evidence is worth stating. The tints come from the same three graders that produced the bars, so the panels are not an independent check on the score. What they add is that the transcripts can be read directly and judged against the score they were given.

The claim drawn from all of this is narrow. The workspace supports the model's propensity to provide rich experiential reports, whether the subject is itself or another entity ([[experiential-report-flattening]]).

The section opens by saying it is difficult to tell whether such reports are grounded in a meaningful internal state or are confabulation, and the experiment does not settle that. It shows the reports depend causally on a particular internal structure. It does not show that they describe that structure correctly. The paper's frame throughout is [[access-consciousness]], a purely functional notion on whose relation to subjective experience it states that it takes no position.

The absence of self-specificity gets an explanation and a hedge in the same sentence. The lack may follow from workspace contents being only weakly tied to the perspective of [[assistant-persona]], though tied nontrivially, as a later section argues ([[assistant-point-of-view]]).

The discussion puts the unablated readout to work once more. [[attention-schema-theory]] predicts that the structure a model reports from carries a description of the operating and not only the content operated on. The thinking-and-feeling readout fits that shape. The paper offers the fit as a fit, among several [[theories-of-consciousness]], rather than as a confirmation.
